lesson.subject: maths
lesson.title: Money
lesson.summary: UK coins and notes, Pakistani rupees, making totals, giving change and shopping stories.
learning_objectives: Name UK coins and Pakistani money

standards.text: Recognise and use symbols for pounds and pence; combine amounts; find change

success_criteria: I can say what each coin is worth
I can add coins to make a total
I can work out change from 50p
lesson.real_life: Pocket money, buying sweets and paying in a shop.

blocks.markdown: Today we use money: coins, totals and change.
blocks.say: Welcome back, number explorer! Today we learn about money. Money is useful every day, for buying a snack or saving up for a toy. We will meet pounds and pence, and rupees too. By the end you will add coins, work out change and shop like a pro.

terms.meaning: Coins and notes used to buy things.

blocks.markdown:
In the UK, 100 **pence** make 1 **pound**.

Coins: 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2. Notes start at £5.
blocks.say: Money helps us buy things. In the United Kingdom people use pounds and pence. A hundred pence make one pound. The coins are one pence, two pence, five pence, ten pence, twenty pence and fifty pence. Then the pound coin and the two pound coin. Bigger numbers on a coin do not always mean a bigger coin. Always read the number!

scenes.caption: 10p, 20p and 50p.
scenes.say: Now bigger coins. Ten pence, twenty pence and fifty pence. A fifty pence coin is worth a lot more than a ten pence coin.

scenes.say: And the pound coins. One pound is one hundred pence. Two pounds is two hundred pence.

blocks.markdown:
In Pakistan people use **rupees**. Coins: Rs 1, 2 and 5. Notes: Rs 10, 20, 50, 100 and more.

Adding money works the same way with pounds or rupees.
blocks.say: In Pakistan people use rupees. The coins are one rupee, two rupees and five rupees. The notes are ten, twenty, fifty, one hundred and bigger. People say a hundred paisa make a rupee, but today we mostly use whole rupees. A friend in Pakistan and a friend in England can both count money. The coins and names are different, but adding works the same way.

blocks.markdown:
To find a **total**, start with the biggest coin and count on.

10p + 5p + 1p + 1p = 17p.
blocks.say: We can make a total by adding coins. Take a ten pence, a five pence and two one pence coins. Start with the biggest. Ten. Add five to make fifteen. Then one more is sixteen, and one more is seventeen. So the total is seventeen pence. Always count the biggest coin first.

scenes.caption: 10p
scenes.say: Start with the biggest coin. Ten pence.

scenes.caption: 10p + 5p = 15p
scenes.say: Add a five pence. Ten, and five more. Fifteen pence.

scenes.caption: 15p + 1p + 1p = 17p
scenes.say: Now two one pence coins. Sixteen. Seventeen. The total is seventeen pence.

blocks.markdown: The same total can be made in different ways: 20p = 10p + 10p, or 10p + 5p + 5p.
blocks.say: Let us practise with real coins, or with buttons pretending to be coins. Make a total of twenty pence in two ways. You could use two ten pence coins. Or one ten, one five and five one pence coins. Different coins can make the same total.

blocks.markdown:
**Change** is the money you get back. Count on from the price to what you paid.

50p - 30p = 20p change.
blocks.say: When we pay with more money than the price, the shop gives us change. A pencil costs thirty pence. We give a fifty pence coin. How much change? Count on from thirty to fifty. Forty, fifty. That is twenty pence. Or take away. Fifty take away thirty is twenty. Twenty pence change.

scenes.say: The pencil costs thirty pence. We hand over a fifty pence coin.

scenes.caption: 50p - 30p = 20p change.
scenes.say: Count on from thirty to fifty. That is a jump of twenty. So the shop gives us twenty pence change.

blocks.say: Now play shopkeeper. Put prices on a few things at home. Ask your family to buy them. Take their coins, add them up, and give the right change. A real shop helps you remember. Which is more fun, buying or selling?

blocks.markdown:
Add the prices to find the **cost**.

20p + 15p = 35p. Pay 50p and get 15p change.
blocks.say: Shopping problems often have two prices. A pencil is twenty pence and a rubber is fifteen pence. How much for both? Add them. Twenty plus fifteen is thirty-five. Thirty-five pence. Can we pay with a fifty pence coin? Yes, because fifty is more than thirty-five. How much change? Fifteen pence.

blocks.markdown:
Zainab has 50p. A drink is 35p and a cake is 20p. 35p + 20p = 55p, which is more than 50p.

No, she cannot buy both.
blocks.say: Zainab has fifty pence. She wants a drink for thirty-five pence and a cake for twenty pence. Can she buy both? Add the prices. Thirty-five plus twenty is fifty-five. That is more than fifty. So no, she cannot buy both. Checking first saves a lot of trouble!
